plot_extraction.response_text:
As a young minister in Balweary, Murdoch Soulis dismisses local superstition and rescues the suspected witch Janet M’Clour from a mob, then employs her at his isolated manse. The next morning Janet appears horribly transformed, with a twisted neck, distorted speech, and an inability to utter God’s name. Although the villagers believe the real Janet is dead and something evil inhabits her body, Soulis attributes her condition to illness and continues protecting her.

During an oppressive summer, Soulis encounters a sinister black man in an old graveyard and pursues him toward the manse, where the stranger mysteriously vanishes. Seeing Janet immediately afterward, Soulis begins to suspect a connection between them and wonders whether she is a demon occupying a corpse.

On the night of August 17, Soulis hears a struggle in Janet’s room and finds her hanging dead from a single nail by a fragile thread. After he locks the room and retreats downstairs, the corpse frees itself, unlocks the door, descends the stairs, and approaches him outside. Soulis confronts it in God’s name and commands it to return to the grave or hell. Lightning strikes the animated corpse, reducing it to ashes as a violent storm breaks. The black man is seen fleeing the district that morning, suggesting that the devil had inhabited Janet’s body and has now been driven away.

Soulis survives but suffers a prolonged breakdown. The ordeal permanently transforms him into a solitary, haunted preacher who annually delivers a terrifying sermon about the devil on the anniversary of the encounter.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the form of a folkloric Gothic tale framed as local history. It begins in measured, formal English with an omniscient account of the aged Reverend Soulis, presenting his haunted appearance and the ominous geography of Balweary before moving backward to the events that shaped him. The principal narrative is then delivered in dense Scots vernacular, as though recounted by an elderly parishioner over a drink. This shift gives the supernatural episode the authority, intimacy, and rough immediacy of oral testimony. The closing return to the minister’s later condition completes the circular structure and turns the entire story into an explanation of an already established mystery.

The prose contrasts elevated literary narration with strongly phonetic dialect. The framing passages use grave, precise, sometimes antiquarian diction, while the embedded tale relies on Scots vocabulary and contractions such as “guidwives,” “bairns,” “gloamin’,” “mirk,” “bogle,” and “deil.” Spellings reproduce speech rather than standardized grammar, and proverbial or communal formulations make the voice sound inherited rather than individually composed. Religious language—biblical titles, references to damnation, prayer, witches, the Accuser, and “the powers of evil”—is interwoven with domestic and regional speech. This gives theology and superstition equal linguistic weight. The repeated description of the mysterious figure as a “black man” belongs to an archaic folkloric convention in which blackness signifies the devil, darkness, and unknowability.

Sentences are often long, cumulative, and rhythmically driven, joining observations with repeated conjunctions. In the vernacular sections, “an’,” “but,” “syne,” and “weel” imitate a storyteller advancing the tale aloud, adding detail after detail while delaying decisive revelation. Parallel constructions and repetitions—especially “whiles,” “there was,” “step by step,” and sequences of increasing numbers or movements—create an incantatory momentum. These flowing sentences are punctuated by abrupt dialogue, exclamations, scriptural challenges, and short declarations at moments of danger. The resulting rhythm alternates between patient accumulation and sudden shock.

The narrative voice is communal and morally opinionated. It frequently invokes what “the folk” thought, what “them that kenned best” believed, and what witnesses later saw. Such collective testimony blurs the distinction between fact, gossip, prejudice, and legend. The narrator anticipates objections, qualifies claims, and addresses the listener directly through expressions such as “ye maun understand,” reproducing the manner of oral storytelling. This voice is not neutral: it shares the parish’s religious assumptions and treats supernatural explanations as credible, even while the young Soulis initially represents educated rationalism. The tension between his intellectual scepticism and the villagers’ inherited belief is central to the story’s dramatic irony.

Characterisation is economical and emblematic. Soulis is first shown as an austere, terrified old preacher, then as a learned but inexperienced young minister whose confidence leaves him vulnerable to realities he dismisses. Janet is constructed largely from communal suspicion, bodily distortion, silence, and uncanny gesture rather than psychological access. Her twisted neck, clicking teeth, crooked grin, and inability to utter God’s name become recurring identifying motifs. The supernatural is therefore expressed through corrupted physical detail: the body resembles a corpse before it is known to be one, and ordinary actions such as washing clothes, walking downstairs, or feeling along a wall become horrifying.

Setting is integral to the style. Place-names such as Balweary, Dule Water, Hanging Shaw, Black Hill, and the Devil’s Hag create a densely localized imaginative world while carrying ominous semantic associations. The manse, causeway, stream, moor, old graveyard, and enclosing trees form a landscape of thresholds between settlement and wilderness, Christianity and older belief, life and death. Spatial description is unusually exact, especially in the opening, allowing later supernatural movement through the house and grounds to feel physically credible. Weather functions as a Gothic pressure system: oppressive heat, breathless darkness, unnatural wind, thunder, and violent rain externalize spiritual disturbance.

Suspense develops through foreshadowing, repetition, and graduated sensory disturbance. The opening announces that Soulis has survived some terror without disclosing it. Later, the black stranger, the circling crows, Janet’s altered body, the minister’s recurring “cauld grue,” the sleepless heat, and unexplained sounds progressively narrow the range of possible explanations. Visual horror is often delayed in favour of sound: stamping feet, a bang, wind moving through the house, an unlocked door opening, and footsteps descending toward the waiting minister. The climactic apparition is revealed slowly and anatomically, after which the pace accelerates into command, lightning, combustion, thunder, rain, and flight.

The tone combines solemnity, dread, grim humour, and theological certainty. Colloquial asides and sardonic observations briefly relieve the tension, but they also strengthen the narrator’s credibility by making the account sound conversational rather than ceremonially “literary.” Horror arises from the collision between mundane village life and absolute spiritual evil. The style ultimately affirms a Calvinistic moral universe in which evil may assume bodily form, rational pride is inadequate, and survival depends upon spiritual courage. Yet the lasting emphasis falls less on triumph than trauma: Soulis defeats the possessing presence, but the encounter permanently transforms him into the wild-eyed preacher introduced at the beginning.

generation.response_text:
## The Seventeenth of August

In the latter years of his ministry, when the Reverend Murdoch Soulis had grown grey in Balweary and the children of those he had baptized were themselves bringing infants to the font, there remained about him a terror which neither time nor prayer had wholly subdued.

He was a tall, spare man, still upright despite his age, with a face that seemed less worn by years than scorched by some inward fire. His eyes, ordinarily lowered and mild, would at moments lift suddenly to an empty doorway or a darkened pane, and then the nearest observer might see in them the fixed attention of one who watches an old enemy. He lived alone, though the parish would gladly have supplied him with a housekeeper; and after sunset no persuasion could induce him to cross the threshold of the manse. If duty called him late to a deathbed, he remained in that house until daylight. He would not travel the moor in darkness, not even with company.

Once in every year, on the seventeenth day of August, he preached concerning the adversary of mankind.

It was no discourse of metaphor, nor any courteous theology concerning temptation and the frailties of the flesh. He spoke of the Devil as of a person known to him: subtle, embodied, watchful, and near. He named him the Accuser, the Father of Lies, the Tenant of Empty Flesh; and his voice, beginning low, would rise until the rafters shook and the people sat rigid in their pews. At the last he always stopped abruptly, with both hands gripping the pulpit, and stared down the aisle as though he saw beyond the church door into a region no other eye could enter.

Then he would say:

“Resist him, though he come wearing the face of one ye have loved. Resist him in the Name.”

Afterward he returned to the manse and barred himself in until morning.

Balweary was not a place likely to lessen such impressions. The village lay in a hollow country between the Black Hill and the Dule Water, with Hanging Shaw darkening the east and a spread of broken moor to the west. The kirk and manse stood apart from the cottages, upon a low rise reached by a stony causeway. Behind the manse was an old burial-ground, long disused, where the grass grew rank among leaning stones; beyond that, the ground fell into a marshy hollow called the Devil’s Hag. The names were older than any written charter, and the people, who knew the histories belonging to them, did not care to explain them after nightfall.

What occurred at Balweary in the first summer of Mr Soulis’s ministry was spoken of for two generations. By then fact, recollection, and warning had been woven together, as they will be in country places. Yet those who doubted might have found it hard to account for the minister’s altered countenance, or for the scorched stone that long remained beside the manse path, or for the strange sermon of every seventeenth of August.

Old Andrew Brodie, who was a herd-laddie in those days and lived to be ninety, told the matter thus.

---

“Aye, ye’ve heard tell o’ Mr Soulis as he was after it,” Andrew would begin, setting down his glass and looking toward the fire. “But ye didna ken him afore. That’s the differ. Ye saw an auld man wi’ the fear o’ God in him, an’ maybe another fear besides; but I mind the young callant that cam’ riding into Balweary wi’ his books tied ahint the saddle an’ his head fu’ o’ learning.

“He wasna abune five-and-twenty, Mr Soulis, an’ as braw a scholar as ever wagged a gown in Embro’. Latin? He had it. Greek? He could ha’e scolded a Greek dominie in his ain tongue. He had logic, philosophy, physic, an’ a hantle o’ new notions about the natural causes o’ things folk had aye kent to be unco. But for a’ his learning, he hadna yet learned that the world’s wider than a library, nor that the deil can quote a clever man’s reasoning back at him.

“The first clash cam’ afore he’d been three weeks in the parish.

“There was an auld wife named Janet M’Clour, that bided in a clay biggin by the Dule. She had been bonnie once, folk said, but gin I mind her she was lean as a winter kail-stalk, wi’ red-rimmed een and a tongue that could strip the bark frae a tree. She gathered simples on the hill, helped at births, laid out the deid, an’ kenned when a coo was bewitched or only eaten ower much wet clover. So, by course, half the parish went to her for aid, and the same half cried witch when the aid went wrang.

“Weel, there came a Sabbath when wee Davie Sanderson took a fit in the kirk-yard. The bairn fell among the graves, girned till his mouth was white, and kicked as though six men were hauling at him. His mother screamed that Janet had overlooked him, for the auld wife had cursed her hens the day afore. That was enough. The guidwives raised a skirl, the men gathered, and in less time than ye could say the Lord’s Prayer they had Janet at the Dule Water, meaning to duck her.

“I was there—no’ helping, mind ye, but a laddie follows a crowd the way a craw follows the plough. They had a rope about her waist, and she was spitting and swearing fit to set the water boiling.

“Then down the brae came Mr Soulis.

“‘What wickedness is this?’ says he.

“‘Justice!’ cried Elspeth Sanderson. ‘The wife has witched my bairn.’

“‘Your bairn suffers from an illness,’ says the minister, ‘and you from ignorance.’

“That didna please them. Ignorance is a complaint few folk will own, though they’ll confess to rheumatism by the hour.

“Tammas Rusk held up the rope. ‘She’ll sink if she’s honest and soom if she’s a witch.’

“‘And if she sinks?’

“‘Then she’s honest.’

“‘And drowned,’ says Mr Soulis.

“He took the rope from Tammas’s hand. There wasna much strength in the minister then, but there was authority, an’ that will whiles lift what muscle canna stir. He rebuked them from Scripture, named murder by its right name, and threatened the magistrate besides. Syne the men began looking at their boots, and the women minded their dinners, and the crowd melted from about the burn.

“Janet stood dripping on the bank, her grey hair clapped to her skull and a look on her face that would sour milk.

“‘You are safe now,’ says Mr Soulis.

“‘Safe?’ says she. ‘An’ wha made me unsafe?’

“‘These foolish accusations.’

“She looked after the folk, then back at him. ‘Ye’re a braw young cock to craw sae loud. See that the nicht doesna wring your neck.’

“‘You should be grateful,’ says he.

“‘Grateful!’ she cried, and laughed till the sound went through me like a saw. ‘Ye’ve ta’en me frae the water. Maybe the water wasna the worst.’

“Now, that was Janet’s way, and there were some said afterward she had given him fair warning. Mr Soulis heard only an embittered old woman. When he learned that her landlord had turned her out and no soul in Balweary would shelter her, what must he do but take her to the manse as housekeeper?

“Ye may smile, but there was courage in it, and charity too. Pride as well, maybe. The young are fond o’ making sermons wi’ their deeds, and Mr Soulis meant the parish to learn that superstition would get no footing under his roof.

“Janet went up the causeway after him, dripping all the road.

“That very nicht the change came upon her.

“Nane could say what happened between sunset and dawn. The minister slept soundly, for he’d ridden far that day, and the manse walls were thick. But about four in the morning Kirstie Low came past wi’ milk from the farm, and she saw Janet standing at the kitchen door.

“Kirstie dropped the pitcher.

“It was Janet’s gown, Janet’s face, Janet’s grey hair; but her head lay over upon her left shoulder as though the neck had been wrung and badly set. One eye looked downward and the other straight ahead. Her mouth was drawn at the corner, and when she tried to speak, the words came thick and broken.

“‘G-guid mornin’, K-kirstie.’

“Kirstie ran screaming to the village.

“By breakfast-time, every soul in Balweary had heard that Janet M’Clour was thrawn. Some said the mob had hurt her. Some said a palsy had struck in the night. But them that kenned best said the true Janet had died before dawn, and something else had lifted her body and put it on like a wet sark.

“Mr Soulis would hear none o’t.

“He examined the woman as far as decency allowed, asked her questions, and concluded that fright, cold, and rough usage had brought on a seizure.

“‘Can ye say the Lord’s name?’ asked old Isobel Pringle, who had come bold as brass to the kitchen.

“Mr Soulis turned on her. ‘Leave my house.’

“‘Let her say it.’

“Janet’s jaw laboured. Her teeth clicked. ‘The—the G-guid—’

“‘His Name,’ says Isobel.

“Janet’s crooked eye rolled toward her, and there came a grin on the slack side of her mouth.

“‘Gae,’ she muttered. ‘Gae doun.’

“‘Say God,’ Isobel demanded.

“Janet made a sound like water bubbling in a drain.

“Mr Soulis put the old woman out himself.

“From that day, Janet kept the manse. She cooked, though Mr Soulis ate little of what she set before him; she swept, though the dust seemed ever to gather behind her; and she washed the minister’s black clothes at the burn, beating them upon the stones while the bairns watched from the far bank. She could say ‘kirk’ and ‘Bible’ and ‘heaven,’ if she tried. But God’s Name never crossed her lips. If challenged, she would grin that sideways grin, and her teeth would click thegither.

“She grew stranger in her gait as the weeks passed. Ye’d see her coming up from the Dule at gloamin’, her basket on one arm, her head lying on her shoulder, and every step set down slow and exact—as if walking was a thing she had learned by watching others. Dogs wouldna pass her on the road. Horses sweated when she came near. Once the minister’s own mare broke its halter and leapt the dyke rather than stand while Janet entered the stable.

“Still Mr Soulis held to his learning.

“‘Animals are sensitive to deformity,’ says he.

“‘Aye,’ says Rob Muir, ‘an’ maybe to something else.’

“‘There is no something else.’

“‘Then ye’ll sleep easy,’ says Rob.

“But whether he slept easy or no, the minister’s face began to alter. He was quieter in company, and twice he asked the beadle if any stranger had been seen about the parish. He preached against credulity; yet he started when the kirk door creaked, and when Janet sat below the pulpit, twisted and still, his eye would find her as a needle finds north.

“Then came the heat.

“I’ve lived through sixty summers since, but never one like that. June dried the burns to threads. July burned the heather grey. The cattle stood knee-deep in the Dule, too weary to crop the bank, and the birds went silent at noon. There was no wind, not on the hill, not among the ash leaves, not even in Hanging Shaw. Day after day the sky hung white over Balweary, and night after night the dark came warm and breathless, wi’ a red smother along the north.

“The folk slept wi’ their doors open, though they barred them fast enough when they heard steps outside.

“For there were steps, or so it was said. A tramp along the moor where no road ran. A foot on the causeway after midnight. A stir in the old graveyard and the crows rising before dawn.

“On the second Tuesday of August, Mr Soulis went to visit a sick woman beyond Black Hill. He returned late, taking the path by the Devil’s Hag, though the folk had warned him against it. The sun was low, red as a furnace mouth, and the old burial-ground lay directly between him and the manse.

“As he came among the stones, he saw a man.

“Mind me: when we spoke of the black man, we meant no traveller from foreign lands. This thing had no nation that God created. It was black the way a hole is black, or a burned tree at midnight. Clothes, face, hands—Mr Soulis could make out no difference among them, save for two pale sparks where the eyes should be.

“The stranger was crouched beside an open grave.

“‘Who are you?’ cried Mr Soulis.

“The black man rose. He was tall—ower tall—and thin, and for one instant he stood with his head bent, listening. Then he turned and ran.

“Mr Soulis was young, and there was anger in him as well as fear. He thought of thieves, resurrection-men, or some rogue seeking to feed the parish tales. So he ran after.

“Away went the black man among the graves, never stumbling. Over the broken wall he went, across the dried marsh, and up toward the manse. Mr Soulis followed, losing ground on the rise but keeping the figure in sight. The stranger reached the garden dyke. He didna climb it. He seemed to pass through the shadow of an elder bush and was gone.

“The minister came up panting.

“There was no gate there, no gap, no place a child could hide. The garden lay bare in the evening light. Behind him was the empty causeway; before him, the manse.

“Then the kitchen door opened.

“Janet stood there.

“Her sleeves were rolled to the elbow. Her hands were wet, and something dark dripped from her fingers to the threshold.

“‘Wha was yon?’ Mr Soulis demanded.

“Janet watched him with the eye that faced forward. ‘Wha—wha was what?’

“‘The man who came this way.’

“‘Nae man.’

“‘I saw him.’

“‘Ye saw—’ Her teeth clicked, once, twice. ‘Ye saw naething.’

“At that the minister felt what he later called the cauld grue: a coldness beginning under the heart and spreading through the body, though the air was hot enough to melt tallow. He looked at Janet’s wet hands. He looked beyond her into the black kitchen. And for the first time he asked himself what manner of illness could twist a neck without killing, still a tongue before one sacred word, and teach a human face to smile like a trap.

“He said nothing more. But that evening he went through his books, not the medical volumes this time, but the older works he had mocked at college: accounts of possession, apparitions, revenants, and the powers of evil. He read until the candle guttered. Whiles he shook his head; whiles he glanced at the ceiling, for Janet’s room was above.

“Next day he went to the burial-ground.

“The grave beside which he had seen the stranger was old and sunken. No earth had been disturbed. Yet on the flat stone at its head were three marks, long and narrow, as if made by fingers pressed into soft clay. The stone itself was hard granite.

“Crows circled overhead, though there was no wind to hold them up.

“From then till the seventeenth, Mr Soulis was seen little in the village. He kept to the manse, reading and praying. Janet moved about him as before, setting his meals down, carrying water, trailing her slow shadow from room to room. He tried her twice with the Name. Once she pretended not to hear. Once she turned upon him so quickly that her neck gave a dry crack, and the sound silenced him.

“On the evening of the seventeenth, the heat was worst of all.

“There was a haze over the Dule, and clouds stood piled behind Black Hill, but no thunder came. The air in the manse was close as a sealed tomb. Mr Soulis ate no supper. Janet sat in the kitchen, her hands folded and her head upon her shoulder, humming through her crooked mouth.

“Near ten, she rose.

“‘I’m awa’ to my bed,’ she said.

“It was the clearest sentence she had spoken since the change.

“Mr Soulis looked up.

“Janet grinned.

“‘A guid nicht to ye, meenister.’

“She went out. Step by step she crossed the passage. Step by step she climbed the stair. At the top she paused, and Mr Soulis, sitting below with the Bible open before him, heard three small sounds:

“Click. Click. Click.

“Her teeth.

“Then the chamber door shut.

“The minister remained in the kitchen. He tried to read the Psalms but found himself following every noise of the house: the settling of wood, the faint scrape of a branch against stone, the ticking of the clock. Eleven passed. Then midnight. Still there was no wind.

“A little after one, he heard a foot stamp overhead.

“Then another.

“Then came a dragging, a thud against the wall, and a low muttering in two voices.

“Two, Mr Soulis swore thereafter, though there was but one creature in the room: one voice thick and broken like Janet’s, the other deep and rapid, speaking no tongue he knew.

“He took the candle and went to the stair.

“The muttering ceased.

“‘Janet?’ he called.

“No answer.

“He climbed. The flame bent though the air was still. At the chamber door he listened. Something inside gave one last violent struggle; the bedstead struck the wall; then all was quiet.

“Mr Soulis lifted the latch.

“The room was empty at first sight. The bedclothes were tossed, the casement open, and the curtain hanging without a stir. Then his candle rose, and he saw her.

“Janet hung from a nail behind the door.

“It was a small nail, scarcely fit to hold a coat, and from it ran a single length of grey worsted no thicker than knitting thread. Yet there she swung, her bare feet a hand’s breadth from the floor, her body turning little by little. Her neck was no longer bent sideways. It was stretched straight and long, and the face beneath it had gone dark.

“Mr Soulis stood frozen.

“Then one of the dead eyes opened.

“Only a fraction. Only enough to show a thread of white.

“He backed out, pulled the door shut, and turned the key. He took the key with him. Downstairs he went—not running, for his knees would scarce obey him—and into the kitchen, where he laid the Bible on the table and tried to pray.

“He couldna.

“The words were there, but his mouth was dry, and his thoughts flew apart like frightened birds. He told himself Janet had taken her life. He told himself the eye had not opened. He told himself the thread might be stronger than it looked and the nail set deeper than appeared.

“Then the wind began.

“It came first within the house, not without. A breath moved down the chimney and scattered cold ashes across the hearth. The kitchen door lifted on its hinges. Papers rustled on the table. Yet through the window he could see the elder bush standing still beneath the heavy sky.

“Above him there came a faint creak.

“The nail, he thought.

“Creak.

“The thread.

“Creak.

“Then a soft sound, like bare feet touching the floor.

“Mr Soulis rose.

“There came a scratch at the chamber door. A pause. Another scratch, lower down, as though fingers were feeling for the latch.

“He had locked it. The key lay on the table before him.

“The latch lifted.

“The chamber door opened.

“Ye maun understand, he heard each thing. No haste, no confusion. First the latch, then the hinge, then a pause on the landing. After that came the steps.

“One.

“A drag.

“Two.

“A drag.

“Three.

“Each stair cried under the weight. Mr Soulis watched the kitchen doorway, and the cauld grue took him so that his teeth knocked in his head.

“Halfway down, the thing stopped.

“A thread gave a little twang in the dark.

“Then the steps came on.

“Four.

“Five.

“Six.

“The minister seized the Bible, but his hand shook and the book fell open upon the floor. He looked toward the outer door. It stood ajar. Whether he chose to flee or whether the Lord drew him forth, he never could say; but he crossed the threshold backward, keeping his face toward the passage, and came into the yard.

“The sky was black now, cloud upon cloud, but still no rain had fallen. A pale, sickly light lay over the causeway. The old graves beyond the dyke seemed to lean nearer.

“Within the manse, the dragging reached the bottom stair.

“A hand appeared around the passage wall.

“It was grey and swollen, the fingers crooked, and about one wrist trailed the broken worsted thread.

“Then came the arm, the shoulder, and Janet’s face.

“Deid she was. There was no deceiving it now. Her neck was lengthened by the rope, her tongue dark between her teeth, her eyes glazed and starting. Yet she walked. Step by step, dragging one foot, she came through the kitchen and turned toward the open door.

“Behind her, high upon the passage wall, her shadow rose in another shape: tall, narrow, and black, with a head that brushed the ceiling.

“Mr Soulis saw it, and knowledge entered him whole.

“This was no sick wife. This was no palsy, no village ignorance, no harmless matter for learned argument. Janet M’Clour was dead—maybe since the night of the Dule, maybe only since the hanging—and a tenant not born of woman had lodged in her flesh.

“The corpse reached the threshold.

“I’ve heard folk say courage means feeling no fear. That’s blethers. A man is courageous when the fear has eaten the marrow of him and still he stands. Mr Soulis was near senseless with terror, but somewhere beneath his learning and pride there remained the faith he had preached before he understood its cost.

“He lifted both hands.

“‘In the Name of God,’ he said.

“The corpse stopped.

“The shadow behind it spread along the wall.

“Janet’s jaws opened. From them came the deep voice he had heard overhead.

“‘He is not here.’

“‘He is everywhere,’ said Mr Soulis.

“The thing took one step.

“‘Ye saved this flesh,’ it said. ‘Ye opened the door.’

“‘I saved a woman from murder.’

“‘An’ gave me a house.’

“Another step. The smell of wet earth came with it, though the ground was dry.

“Mr Soulis’s voice broke, but he raised it again.

“‘Whatever ye are, ye have no claim here.’

“The corpse smiled, and the stretched neck bent gradually sideways until the head rested once more upon the shoulder.

“‘Nae claim?’ it said. ‘She cursed Him. She called me. They drove her to the water, and ye—ye proud bairn wi’ your books—ye took my hand and led me hame.’

“At that the minister nearly yielded, for the words struck where his guilt lay hidden. But from the open Bible at his feet a phrase returned to him—not as print upon a page, but as a command remembered from before memory.

“Resist.

“He stepped toward the corpse.

“‘Janet M’Clour, if aught of you remains, the Lord have mercy upon your soul. But you that use her—hear me.’

“The thing recoiled.

“Mr Soulis pointed past it, toward the burial-ground and the dark hollow of the Hag.

“‘Go back to the grave, if the grave will hold ye. Go down to hell, if hell will take ye. By the Blood, by the Word, by the Name ye cannot speak, I command ye—depart!’

“Janet’s body sprang at him.

“At that same instant the whole world turned white.

“There was no space between flash and stroke. Lightning came down upon the yard with a noise that split the night. Mr Soulis was hurled against the dyke. The manse windows burst outward. Every bell in the kirk began ringing without a hand.

“And where the corpse had stood there rose a pillar of blue flame.

“It burned for no more than a breath. Then the rain fell—great warm drops at first, then sheets of water driven by a wind that tore limbs from the ashes and flattened the heather on the hill. Thunder went rolling over Balweary, stroke upon stroke, and the Dule rose black between its banks.

“The folk found Mr Soulis at dawn, crouched beside the causeway with the Bible clasped to his breast. He could not speak. His hair, that had been brown the day before, was marked with a broad streak of white.

“Of Janet there remained only ashes, grease upon the stones, two iron buckles from her shoes, and the little grey thread.

“That same morning Rob Muir and three others saw the black man crossing the crest of Black Hill. The storm was still breaking, and he went against the wind with such speed that no living man could have kept his feet. When he reached the standing stones, he turned once toward Balweary.

“Then the rain hid him.

“No trace was found beyond the hill.”

---

For many weeks Murdoch Soulis lay between fever and insensibility. When speech returned, he spoke first in Latin, then in fragments of Scripture, and only after some months could he give any connected account of the night. Even then he would not name all that he had seen. The chamber in which Janet died was stripped and sealed; later, when the manse roof required rebuilding, Soulis ordered that entire portion of the house pulled down.

He resumed his ministry, but the young scholar who had ridden into Balweary did not resume it with him. His contempt for the old beliefs was gone, though he never encouraged cruelty against any suspected witch, seer, or unfortunate outcast. Indeed, he preached more fiercely than before against the violence of crowds. Superstition, he said, might be a lie; but pride was another lie, and sometimes the Devil entered by the door a man had opened merely to display his wisdom.

He never married. He kept no servant overnight. Those who visited the manse found iron lamps burning in every passage and a Bible laid open beside each door. Yet children loved him in daylight, and the sick called for him willingly, for no minister in the district was more gentle with mortal fear.

Only after dark did his face assume that listening look.

And once each year, upon the seventeenth of August, the people of Balweary came from the Dule Water, Hanging Shaw, the Black Hill, and the farms beyond the Devil’s Hag. They filled the kirk before sunset and waited in silence while the aged minister climbed the pulpit stair.

Outside, perhaps, the evening would be fair. The moor might lie purple and quiet; the ash leaves might scarcely stir. But before Soulis had spoken ten minutes, the congregation would imagine the oppression of that ancient heat, the open grave, the slow foot upon the stair, and the dead hand feeling along the wall.

Then the minister’s eyes would fix upon the dark beneath the gallery, and his voice would deepen.

“The powers of evil,” he would say, “are not made harmless because ye give them softer names. Nor is the Lord absent because your courage fails. I have stood where reason left me. I have seen the Tenant in the empty house.”

At these words the oldest parishioners bowed their heads, remembering what their fathers had told them; and the youngest, though they understood nothing, ceased to move.

Soulis would lean forward, his white hands trembling on the pulpit.

“If it come with threats, resist it. If it come with promises, resist it. If it come wearing pity, resist it. And if it come wearing a kent face and speaking with a kent tongue—look not to the face, but call upon the Name.”

Then, from somewhere in the settling kirk, there would sometimes come a small dry sound, no more than the click of shrinking timber.

At that sound the Reverend Murdoch Soulis always stopped.

And every soul in Balweary stopped with him.

Mara Vale repaired clocks in a town where no one was ever late.

Every morning at seven, the bakery opened. At seven ten, the milk cart rattled over the eastern bridge. At eight, the school bell rang twice, and at eight fifteen, Mayor Bell crossed the square carrying a black umbrella, whether it rained or not. Even the gulls seemed to wheel above the harbor according to a schedule posted somewhere in the clouds.

The town was called Bellwether, and at its center stood the Great Clock.

It had four white faces, each wide as a house, and hands of hammered copper that flashed green in the sun. Beneath the clock faces, behind walls of gray stone, hung a pendulum taller than three men. Its swing governed every watch, bell, oven, ferry, and appointment in town.

At least, that was what people said.

Mara’s shop stood in the clock tower’s shadow. Over the door, a wooden sign read VALE & DAUGHTER, though her father had been dead for nine years and there had never been another daughter. She kept the sign because the gold lettering was still good.

Inside, hundreds of clocks ticked at different volumes. Brass carriage clocks, walnut mantel clocks, painted cuckoo clocks, silver watches, iron alarm clocks, and one tiny clock set inside a glass ring all spoke at once. Visitors often found the sound overwhelming. Mara heard it as weather.

On the first Monday of October, at precisely nine minutes past ten, a stranger brought her a clock that did not tick.

He was old, though not in the ordinary way. His coat was carefully mended, his boots were dusty, and his hair was white except for one black strand above his left ear. He placed a small wooden box on her counter.

“I need this repaired,” he said.

Mara opened the lid.

Inside lay a pocket watch of dark metal. Its case was engraved with a bird in flight. There were no numbers on its face, only a single black hand pointing upward.

“It has no winding crown,” Mara said.

“No.”

“No hinge on the back.”

“No.”

“And only one hand.”

“Yes.”

“Then how am I supposed to open it?”

The stranger smiled. “At the right time.”

Mara disliked riddles before lunch.

“What’s wrong with it?”

“It stopped.”

“So I gathered.”

“Can you make it go again?”

“Perhaps. Who made it?”

“You did.”

The shop seemed to become louder. A dozen pendulums swung. A cuckoo called once from the wall, although the hour was nowhere near.

Mara looked at the stranger. “I’ve never seen this watch before.”

“Not yet.”

She nearly pushed the box back to him. Then she noticed the engraving beneath the bird: a small letter V crossed by a line. It was her mark, the signature she scratched into every mechanism she built.

The mark was imperfect. The left stroke leaned too far outward, exactly as hers always did.

“Where did you get this?”

The stranger glanced toward the window. Outside, townspeople crossed the square in neat streams. Above them, the Great Clock showed ten thirteen.

“You gave it to me,” he said. “A long time from now.”

Mara shut the lid.

“Get out.”

“At noon tomorrow, the Great Clock will lose one minute.”

“The Great Clock has not lost a minute in two hundred and six years.”

“I know.”

“And you expect me to believe you came from the future?”

“No,” said the stranger. “I expect you to believe the clock.”

He left the box on the counter and walked out.

Mara hurried after him, but when she reached the street, he was gone. There was nowhere he could have hidden. The square was broad and bare, and every shop door was closed against the autumn wind.

At ten fifteen, Mayor Bell passed under the tower with his umbrella.

Mara took the dark watch into her workshop and tried every tool she owned. The metal resisted files. Oil rolled off it. Magnets had no effect. When she held it to her ear, she heard no mechanism, only a faint rushing sound like waves in a shell.

She worked until midnight.

Before going to bed in the room above the shop, she placed the watch inside her father’s old safe. Then she locked the safe, locked the workshop, locked the shop, and slept badly.

In her dream, the whole town stood knee-deep in black water. The people stared at the clock tower while fish swam through open windows. The Great Clock’s hands spun backward, and somewhere beneath the water a man knocked against glass.

The next morning, the dark watch lay on her bedside table.

Mara sat up so quickly she struck her head on the wall.

The safe downstairs was still locked. So were the workshop and shop doors. She examined the watch again. The single hand now pointed slightly to the right.

At eleven fifty-five, Mara carried it into the square.

She felt foolish. The sky was clear. Shopkeepers stood in doorways, enjoying the cold sunlight. Children marched back to school after their midday meal. The milk cart returned over the bridge. Everything happened as it always had.

At noon, the tower bell began to ring.

One.

Two.

Three.

Mara counted each stroke.

At twelve, the final note rolled over the rooftops and out across the harbor.

The Great Clock read eleven fifty-nine.

For a moment, no one moved.

Then the minute hand jumped forward.

The baker laughed uncertainly. A teacher clapped as if a trick had been performed. People checked their watches and found them correct. The Great Clock showed noon again.

Conversation resumed. Carts rolled. Doors shut. Within five minutes, the square had returned to order.

Only Mara remained still.

The dark watch’s single hand had moved another fraction to the right.

That afternoon, Mayor Bell entered her shop.

He was a tall, narrow man with a silver beard and a manner so polished that even his anger seemed ceremonial. His black umbrella hung from one arm.

“I understand you were in the square at noon,” he said.

“So were many people.”

“You were watching the tower.”

“I often watch clocks. It’s my profession.”

The mayor did not smile. “Did anyone speak to you about the Great Clock?”

Mara thought of the stranger. “Why would they?”

“An idle question.”

“From a busy man?”

He examined the clocks on her walls, none of which required repair. “Your father cared for the tower mechanism.”

“He did.”

“And after his death, the council appointed Mr. Quill.”

“Mr. Quill oils what he can reach and lies about the rest.”

“Nevertheless, you are not authorized to enter the tower.”

“I haven’t tried.”

“Good.”

The mayor turned to leave.

“Why did the clock lose a minute?” Mara asked.

His hand tightened around the umbrella.

“Old machines,” he said, “occasionally surprise us.”

“So do old men.”

Mayor Bell looked back at her. For an instant, his expression was not angry but afraid.

Then he left.

At closing time, Mara found a folded piece of paper beneath the dark watch. She had not put it there.

The note contained four words:

BELOW THE PENDULUM. MIDNIGHT.

At eleven forty-five, Mara locked her shop and crossed the square.

The tower’s main entrance was guarded at night, but Mara knew another way in. As a child, she had followed her father through a drain tunnel beside the canal. The tunnel smelled worse than she remembered and was narrower than it had been when she was twelve, but it still ended behind a loose grate in the tower cellar.

She emerged into darkness filled with machinery.

The Great Clock’s mechanism occupied nine floors. Gears turned in the walls. Chains vanished into shafts. Counterweights rose and fell with grave patience. At the center, the pendulum swung through the tower like a golden blade.

Mara stood beneath it.

At midnight, the bells shook dust from the ceiling.

On the final stroke, the dark watch opened.

Its back unfolded into six metal petals. Inside, instead of springs and wheels, a disk of pale glass shone with blue light. Lines appeared across it, forming a map of the tower cellar.

A red point blinked beneath Mara’s feet.

She found the trapdoor under a layer of coal dust.

Below it, a spiral staircase descended farther than the tower foundations should have allowed. The air grew warm as Mara followed it down. At the bottom, she reached an iron door bearing the seal of Bellwether: a sheep with a bell around its neck.

The door was unlocked.

Beyond it stood a vast underground chamber.

Mara forgot to breathe.

Hundreds of glass cylinders rose from floor to ceiling. Copper tubes connected them in a shining web. Within each cylinder floated something that looked like smoke underwater—silver, restless, alive. Labels had been fixed to the glass.

APRIL 3, 1791—ELEVEN MINUTES.

DECEMBER 19, 1834—THREE HOURS.

JULY 8, 1880—TWO DAYS.

Some cylinders were small enough to hold in one hand. Others were wider than houses.

At the center of the chamber, pipes descended from the Great Clock into a black reservoir. A gauge on its side trembled near a red mark.

“You came.”

The stranger stepped from behind the reservoir.

Mara raised the dark watch like a weapon. “Who are you?”

“Jonas Vale.”

Her mouth went dry.

“My son,” she whispered.

“Eventually.”

“I don’t have a son.”

“Not yet.”

The stranger—Jonas—looked up at the cylinders. Blue light deepened the lines in his face.

“What is this place?”

“The reason no one in Bellwether is ever late.”

He touched a cylinder labeled MAY 14, 1902—TWENTY-SEVEN MINUTES.

“The Great Clock does not measure time,” he said. “It takes it.”

Mara waited.

“Small amounts, usually. A second from a conversation. Five minutes from a walk. An hour from someone’s sleep. The machine smooths the stolen time across the town. It keeps ships on schedule, prevents accidents, delays storms, and ensures that every harvest comes before the first frost.”

“That’s impossible.”

“You are standing under a tower full of stolen Tuesdays.”

She looked again at the silver currents trapped in glass.

“Where does it come from?”

“Everyone. No one notices a few seconds. When more is needed, the council takes larger pieces.”

Mara remembered her father in his final months. He had been fifty-three, strong and loud, with hands that could straighten a bent gear by touch. Then, in a single winter, he had become ancient. His hair whitened. His back curved. By spring, he was dead.

“What did they take from my father?”

Jonas lowered his eyes.

“How much?”

“Seventeen years.”

The chamber blurred.

Mara gripped the edge of the reservoir until its bolts cut her palm. “Why?”

“He discovered the machine was failing. Mayor Bell demanded that he repair it. Your father refused. He said the town had lived too long on borrowed time.”

“And Bell took his life?”

“Bell’s father did. The mayors are all from the same family. They’ve guarded this place for generations.”

Above them, the mechanism groaned.

The gauge’s needle jumped closer to the red mark.

“What happens when that reaches the end?” Mara asked.

“The reservoir breaks. All the stored time returns at once.”

“To the people it was taken from?”

“To everything.”

She imagined buildings aging into dust, children becoming adults in a heartbeat, dead trees blooming and rotting, waves freezing over the harbor and racing away.

“When?”

“Tomorrow at noon.”

“The clock lost one minute today.”

“The first crack in the reservoir. It will lose an hour in the morning. Then everything.”

Mara stared at him. “Why come to me?”

“Because you made the watch.”

“You keep saying that.”

“In my time, Bellwether no longer exists. The clock failed when I was a child. You saved me by putting me on a boat before the collapse, but you stayed behind.”

Jonas took the watch from her gently.

“Years later, I found this among your tools. It can move against the current of time, but only once in each direction. I used it to come here.”

“Then we warn the town.”

“They won’t believe us.”

“We show them the chamber.”

“Mayor Bell will stop us.”

“Then we stop him first.”

Jonas smiled, and for an instant Mara saw something of herself in his face.

“That,” he said, “is what you said before.”

Footsteps rang on the staircase.

Mayor Bell entered the chamber with six guards.

“I had hoped,” he said, “that grief had taught you not to interfere with the tower.”

The guards surrounded Mara and Jonas. Each carried a short iron club.

Mara looked at the mayor. “You knew this would happen.”

“I knew the machine required adjustment.”

“It is about to burst.”

“Mr. Quill assures me the reservoir can be stabilized.”

“Mr. Quill thinks a differential gear is a disease of the liver.”

The mayor’s jaw tightened.

Jonas stepped forward. “You need to empty the reservoir gradually. Release the stored time before noon.”

“Into what?” asked Bell.

“The town.”

“Absolutely not.”

“Then the town dies.”

The mayor walked to a cylinder and laid one hand against the glass.

“You see theft,” he said. “I see two centuries without famine. Ships that returned before storms. Children pulled from roads before runaway carts arrived. Fires that burned slowly enough to be extinguished. Bellwether prospers because the clock gives us what the rest of the world lacks: order.”

“It killed my father,” Mara said.

“It saved thousands.”

“You always say thousands when you mean yourself.”

For the first time, Bell’s composure broke.

“My family has given more than any other. Do you imagine the machine runs without judgment? Every day we choose where seconds must be added and where they can be removed. Every day we carry the burden of keeping this town alive.”

“No,” said Jonas. “You carry an umbrella.”

One of the guards laughed before turning it into a cough.

Mayor Bell struck Jonas across the face.

Jonas fell against the reservoir. The gauge needle shuddered into the red.

A thin crack appeared in the black metal.

Silver light spilled through it.

All at once, Mara remembered a day that had never happened.

She stood on the harbor pier holding a red-haired baby. Her son. Jonas. He grabbed her finger and laughed as gulls cried overhead.

The memory vanished.

Another took its place: her father teaching her to polish brass; a summer evening stretched warm and endless; her mother singing in a kitchen that had been torn down twenty years ago.

The stolen time was leaking.

Everyone in the chamber felt it. A guard dropped his club and began to weep. Another gasped the name of someone he had forgotten.

The mayor stared at his hands. For a moment, they appeared young.

Then the crack sealed itself.

Silence returned.

Mara understood.

“The time wants to go back,” she said.

Jonas rose, blood on his lip. “Yes.”

“The pipes can reverse.”

“The main escapement must be disengaged.”

“From the clock room.”

Mayor Bell motioned to the guards. “Take them.”

The tower lurched.

Far above, bells rang once.

Then again.

Then a third time, too quickly.

Everyone looked up.

“It’s begun,” Jonas said.

Mara threw the dark watch at the nearest lamp.

Glass shattered. Oil flared across the floor. In the sudden confusion, she seized a guard’s club and struck the valve beside the reservoir. Steam burst into the chamber. Jonas tackled another guard. Mayor Bell shouted orders no one obeyed.

Mara ran.

She climbed the spiral stairs two at a time. The tower mechanism hammered around her. Gears spun too fast. Chains whipped through pulleys. On the fourth floor, she saw the minute hand’s enormous axle turning backward.

Outside, the town screamed.

Through a window, Mara glimpsed chaos in the square. People staggered as lost seconds returned. A woman dropped a basket, then caught it before it fell, then dropped it again. A cart crossed the same patch of road three times. Autumn leaves rose from the gutters and fastened themselves to branches.

Mara climbed higher.

At the clock room, Mr. Quill knelt beside the escapement, turning a wrench in the wrong direction.

“Stop!” she shouted.

He looked up. “The mayor ordered—”

A gear tooth snapped and flew past his head.

Mr. Quill fainted.

The main escapement stood behind the pendulum shaft: a steel lever controlling the release of the entire mechanism. Mara pulled it. It did not move.

A keyhole sat at its base.

The dark watch.

She had left it below.

The stairs shook as Jonas stumbled into the room.

He held the watch.

“Thought you might need this.”

Behind him came Mayor Bell, carrying a guard’s club.

“You do not know what you are releasing,” Bell said.

“I know exactly what was taken,” Mara replied.

“You’ll destroy everything we built.”

“Then we’ll build it again honestly.”

Bell raised the club. Jonas moved between them.

The mayor swung.

Mara caught his arm, but the blow struck Jonas’s shoulder. The dark watch fell and skidded beneath the pendulum. Mara dived after it. The copper blade swept over her, close enough to lift her hair.

She seized the watch.

Its petals opened as she brought it near the keyhole. The single black hand pointed straight down.

The watch fitted perfectly.

Mayor Bell tore free from Jonas and rushed toward her.

Mara turned the key.

The escapement released.

The Great Clock stopped.

For the first time in two hundred and six years, Bellwether was silent.

Then every cylinder beneath the tower shattered.

Time rose through the mechanism in a silver flood. It poured from windows, burst through clock faces, and rolled across the town without heat or sound.

Mara saw her father standing beside the pendulum. He was young, his beard still red, his eyes bright with pride.

“You found it,” he said.

She reached for him.

The wave struck.

Morning and evening passed in the same breath. The tower walls cracked, healed, and cracked again. Bells became green with age, then shone as new. Mara felt seconds entering her: forgotten meals, unfinished dreams, pauses between words, hours taken from sleep. She lived a hundred small moments all at once.

She saw Jonas as a child.

She saw herself hiding him aboard a fishing boat beneath a gray, broken sky.

She saw years that might never come.

Then the silver light vanished.

Mara lay on the clock room floor.

Sunlight entered through the western clock face. The hands had stopped at twelve.

Jonas sat nearby, no longer old. He looked about thirty. The white had gone from his hair, including the single black strand that had once remained.

Mayor Bell leaned against the wall. His beard was dark, but his face was full of bewilderment. In one instant, decades of inherited memories had returned to him: choices made by fathers, grandfathers, and mayors whose names were carved beneath the tower. He lowered the club.

“What time is it?” he asked.

No one answered.

Below, the people of Bellwether emerged into the square.

The bakery opened late the next morning.

The milk cart did not arrive at all because the horse had wandered into an orchard and refused to leave. School began at nine twenty-three, though the teacher claimed it was nine fifteen. The ferry departed without three passengers and returned for them. Mayor Bell crossed the square at noon carrying no umbrella, only to be caught in the first rain.

At first, the town hated it.

People missed meetings. Bread burned. Fishermen argued over tides. Watches disagreed. The great hands on the tower remained fixed, and no one could decide whether to repair them.

But no storms paused at the harbor after that. No harvest waited politely for the farmers. Accidents happened, as did narrow escapes. Children grew at the proper speed. Old people complained that years passed too quickly, and young people complained that they passed too slowly.

Mara kept the dark watch in her workshop.

Jonas stayed through winter. They spoke carefully about the future, like travelers comparing maps of a country whose borders were changing. He told her nothing about his father. Mara did not ask. Some doors, she decided, should remain closed until one reached them.

In spring, the watch’s black hand began to point upward again.

“It’s time,” Jonas said.

They stood on the eastern bridge at dawn. Gulls wheeled above the harbor without apparent instruction.

“Will you remember me?” Mara asked.

“I think so.”

“Will I still have you?”

Jonas smiled. “I think that depends on whether you’re late.”

He pressed the watch into her hand.

“I made this for you,” she said.

“You will.”

The metal petals opened. Blue light wrapped around him.

Mara wanted to say something wise, something a mother might say at the end of a long life. But she had not yet become his mother, and her life was not ending.

So she said, “Take care of your shoulder.”

Jonas laughed.

Then he was gone.

Years later, Mara married a boatbuilder who had once missed the ferry because his horse wandered into an orchard. Their son was born red-haired and loud on a rainy afternoon. They named him Jonas, though Mara never explained why.

The Great Clock was not repaired.

Vines climbed the tower. Birds nested behind its frozen hands. The underground chamber was emptied, its broken cylinders melted down and made into bells for ships and schools and front doors.

Mara’s shop remained full of ticking.

Above the entrance, the old sign still read VALE & DAUGHTER, though she had a son and no daughter. She kept it because the gold lettering was still good, and because people no longer expected every sign, clock, promise, or life to be perfectly accurate.

Sometimes a customer would hurry in, apologizing for being late.

Mara always smiled.

“For what?” she would ask.
